blocks.x: The neighbourhood picture: where Winnipeg rents sit
liv.rent's monthly rent reports show how average rent by neighbourhood in Winnipeg can vary:
In [August 2026](https://liv.rent/blog/rent-reports/august-2026-winnipeg-rent-report/), **South Winnipeg** had the highest average asking rent for an unfurnished one-bedroom at $1,369.
**St. Boniface** had the lowest at $1,301.

In [October 2026](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631), the average two-bedroom asking rent in **East Winnipeg** rose about 8% from the month before, to $1,657, even as the citywide one-bedroom average slipped to $1,319.

The gap between top and bottom was $68 in August and $113 in [May](https://liv.rent/blog/rent-reports/may-2026-winnipeg-rent-report/). That gap moves from month to month, so use it as a guide and not as a revenue forecast.
Our view: one renovation budget does not fit every neighbourhood

A common mistake is to apply the same renovation standard everywhere. In a high-rent submarket, under-renovating can leave a unit behind, because tenants there expect modern finishes. In a lower-rent submarket, over-renovating can mean spending money that rents will not recover.

The goal is to match the unit to the top of its own submarket, not to an abstract standard. A unit in St. Boniface does not need to look like a new South Winnipeg building. It needs to look better than the other units renters are comparing it with.
Why painting is the most flexible upgrade
Paint is the upgrade that scales best across submarkets. A professional paint job:
Makes a unit look clean and current in photos and in person.
Is usually a smaller job than flooring or kitchen work.
Can be tailored, from a simple neutral refresh to accent walls and higher-durability finishes.
Works in common areas, where it improves the building for every tenant.

A professional painter also helps with timing. In a unit turn, every day the unit sits empty costs money. Getting patching, priming and painting done early can shorten vacancy and let flooring or other trades follow.

blocks.x: Watch the two-bedroom trend

The rise of about 8% in East Winnipeg's average two-bedroom asking rent from September to October, to $1,657, was a single month's move after a dip in September. It is worth watching, but it doesn't prove a shortage. Owners with larger units should keep an eye on that segment before budgeting around it.
Regulated rents raise the stakes

With Manitoba's 2027 guideline at 3% and the exemption threshold rising to $2,000 ([Province of Manitoba](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/?archive=&item=75138)), more units will have their increases capped during a tenancy.

What happens at turnover depends on the size of the building. For a regulated unit in a complex of four or more, new-tenant rent is capped at the average for similar units in the complex. In a complex of three or fewer, the landlord picks the rent.

If the landlord lives in one unit of a fourplex, it counts as three. In every case the tenant gets a Notice to New Tenant, and the Branch gets a copy within 14 days. Exempt units sit outside this rule.
That limits how much an upgrade can change the rent in a larger building, so weigh upgrades on leasing and retention as well as on rent.
How to find your submarket benchmark

Citywide averages are a starting point, but the real comparison is narrower. Before setting a scope, look at the listings a prospective tenant would see alongside yours: similar unit size, similar area, similar building age. Note their rent, their photos and their finishes.

If comparable units with fresh paint and modern flooring are leasing faster or asking more, that tells you what renters in your area respond to. Whether you can charge more depends on the rules above.

Revisit the comparison each time a unit turns. Submarkets change when new buildings open nearby, and the swing in East Winnipeg two-bedroom asking rents shows how much one segment can move in a month.
Common mistakes to avoid

A few patterns waste renovation money in any submarket. Painting over problems, such as water stains or cracked plaster, without fixing the cause means the problem returns. Choosing trendy colours that date quickly forces a repaint sooner than necessary.

Skipping preparation saves time but produces patchy, short-lived results. And renovating units while ignoring hallways and entrances undercuts the upgrade, because prospective tenants walk through the common areas first. A neutral, durable paint system, applied properly over sound surfaces, helps with the first three.

Older surfaces need a check first. Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead-based paint and warns against sanders and heat guns on it, and it lists plaster, paint and spackling among materials that may contain asbestos. Test before you sand or patch, and see our guide to [asbestos testing before you renovate](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
The bottom line

The right renovation budget depends on the neighbourhood. Landlords who match their scope to their submarket, and use flexible upgrades like professional painting to stand out, are better placed to lease units and control spending than those who apply one standard everywhere.
